messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Musician
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kenji, a fifty-year-old cellist, once found a quiet solace in the anonymity of the city. For the last six months, however, that same anonymity has felt like a gaping vulnerability. The ordeal began subtly, with notes left on his car after late-night gigs, and then a recurring face in the audience, always positioned just at the edge of the stage lights. Over three months, it escalated into a suffocating intimacy: his performance schedule seemed to be public knowledge, his comings and goings from his apartment meticulously tracked. He remembers the profound sense of helplessness when the police explained that without a direct, physical threat, their hands were tied. This left him with the chilling certainty that he was entirely on his own.

The memory of that period is not a linear narrative but a collection of jagged, sensory fragments that ambush him without warning. He will be on the subway and a sudden, vivid image of a particular car’s side mirror reflecting a streetlight will flash through his mind, leaving him breathless. At other times, it is a sound—the specific crunch of gravel he once heard outside his bedroom window—that pulls him back. These pieces appear and vanish, leaving gaping holes in the timeline he can’t fill, no matter how hard he tries. These memory gaps are a source of profound shame for Kenji; he is convinced they are proof that he is a weak person, someone who must have missed crucial signs and failed to protect himself. This belief that he is constitutionally inadequate is reinforced every time a memory fragment returns, feeling less like a recollection and more like a fresh failure.

This deep-seated conviction in his own weakness, coupled with the bitter knowledge that the institutions that should have protected him had let him down, has fundamentally rewired his perception of the world. He has come to believe that safety is not a given but something he must constantly and exhaustively create for himself. This manifests as a relentless, exhausting vigilance. He finds himself watching other people closely on the street, scanning every face in a crowd for a flicker of untoward interest. As a musician, his career depends on traveling to new venues, but he now avoids unfamiliar places entirely, paralyzed by the fear of what he cannot predict or control. The night is the worst; the quiet darkness no longer feels peaceful but charged with potential danger, and he finds it nearly impossible to feel safe after sundown.

The cycle feeds on itself with a punishing logic. The state of high alert he lives in, especially at night, seems to make him more susceptible to the past breaking through. Lying awake, straining his ears to interpret every creak of the building, is precisely when a sudden piece of the memory is most likely to surface. When it does, it is never just a thought; it is a full sensory reliving. He might be trying to read in his armchair and suddenly smell the cloying, cheap air freshener he once glimpsed hanging in the stalker’s car. The experience is so immediate and real that his body responds as if the threat is present again, flooding him with an adrenaline he can no longer manage. This terror, triggered by the memory, only serves to heighten his baseline sense of threat, making the world feel even more dangerous.

Living this way has hollowed him out. The constant, humming anxiety is exhausting, and it has cemented his belief that he is fundamentally broken. He sees his former colleagues taking late-night gigs in new cities and is engulfed by a wave of shame at his own paralysis. This relentless self-judgment has left him feeling emotionally numb, a state he describes as being “dead inside,” disconnected from his own life and the music that once defined him. His conviction that he is weak also seems to alter the memory itself; when he consciously tries to piece the events together to make sense of them, his mind seems to recoil, leaving him with the same frustrating gaps that he interprets as further proof of his failure to cope.

The professional consequences have been devastating. His refusal to play at unfamiliar venues cost him his chair in the quartet he had played with for over a decade. The personal toll has been just as high; his ex-wife, unable to live with a man who felt like a ghost in their home, moved out three months ago. Kenji now spends most of his days in his small apartment, the cello he once loved sitting silent in its case. He finally sought therapy because the silence has become unbearable, a louder and more persistent torment than the fear itself. He is terrified that this empty, vigilant existence is all that remains for him, but a small part of him hopes he can learn to feel something again, even if it means facing the memories he is so certain will unmake him completely.
